title: Using iter(), next() and StopIteration
learningObjectives: Explain the main ideas in using iter(), next() and stopiteration.
Use the relevant iterator or generator protocol correctly.
Trace values and state across successive iteration steps.
Recognize exhaustion, lazy evaluation and relevant edge cases.
Apply the concept to a practical sequence-processing task.

understand.concept: iter() obtains an iterator from an iterable, and next() requests its next value. When the iterator is exhausted, next() raises StopIteration unless a default value is supplied. These operations expose the mechanics normally handled automatically by a for loop.
understand.whyItMatters: Manual iteration is useful when a program needs controlled, step-by-step consumption, lookahead patterns or a clear understanding of lazy data sources.
understand.analogy: iter() gives you a numbered ticket dispenser, and next() requests the next ticket in sequence.
understand.analogyLimit: The ticket analogy does not imply random access or guaranteed finite data. An iterator may be infinite, may perform work when advanced, and may have side effects.

explain.narrative:
## Obtain and advance an iterator
Call `iterator = iter(iterable)` to obtain an iterator. Each call to `next(iterator)` requests one item and advances the iterator. The iterator stores its own progress; calling `next()` again does not return the same item unless the iterator is explicitly designed to do so.

## Handle exhaustion
When no item remains, `next(iterator)` raises `StopIteration`. You can provide a default: `next(iterator, default)` returns that default instead of raising when the iterator is exhausted. A for loop handles StopIteration internally, so application code usually does not need to catch it for ordinary loops.

## One-pass caution
Do not assume an iterator can be rewound. If you need another pass, keep the original reusable iterable or create a new iterator from it.

examples.title: Read values one at a time
examples.explanation: Each next call returns one value and moves the iterator forward.

examples.title: Use a default at exhaustion
examples.explanation: The first call returns the item; the second returns the supplied default instead of raising StopIteration.

examples.title: Consume the remaining values
examples.explanation: After next consumes 2, converting the remaining iterator to a list consumes only the unvisited values.

examples.title: Show an iterator is one-pass
examples.explanation: The first list conversion exhausts the iterator; the second sees no remaining values.

examples.title: Use a for loop instead of manual next calls
examples.explanation: The for loop repeatedly advances the iterator and handles StopIteration automatically.

practise.guidedTask: Write a small program that demonstrates using iter(), next() and stopiteration. Show at least two iteration steps and explain how the state changes.
practise.independentTask: Build a reusable or one-pass sequence processor using this topic. Test normal input, an empty or exhausted case, and describe when each value is calculated.
hints: Identify whether the object is an iterable, an iterator or both.
Write down the state before and after each next() call.
Use StopIteration as the normal completion signal.
Test an empty input and an already exhausted iterator.
Choose a list only when repeated access or storage is required.
practise.challenge: Process a larger sequence incrementally and compare the memory and reuse trade-offs with building a list first.

Returns the first item every time
questions.explanation: next requests one item from the iterator's current position.

questions.prompt: What happens when next(it) is called on an exhausted iterator without a default?
questions.explanation: StopIteration signals that there are no more items.

questions.prompt: What does next(it, 'done') return after exhaustion?
questions.explanation: The optional default is returned instead of raising StopIteration.

questions.prompt: After list(it) consumes an iterator, what will another list(it) normally produce?
options: A duplicate of the first list
questions.explanation: The first conversion exhausts the iterator, leaving no values for the second conversion.

questions.prompt: Which construct normally handles iterator exhaustion automatically?
questions.explanation: A for loop stops cleanly when the iterator raises StopIteration.
